<meta>continues from previous page: it is not of royal dignity</meta>
to exercise authority over beggars, but rather over the wealthy and prosperous. This was certainly the sentiment of Fabricius <note>Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, a Roman consul famous for his austerity and integrity who refused bribes from the Samnites</note>, a man of noble and elevated spirit, when he responded that he would rather rule over the rich than be rich himself. Indeed, for one person to wallow in pleasure and luxury while everyone else is groaning and lamenting is to be the keeper of a prison, not a kingdom.

In short, just as a doctor is most unskilled if he cannot cure a disease except by causing another disease, so he who knows no other way to reform the lives of his citizens than by depriving them of life’s comforts must admit he does not know how to rule free men. Let him instead shake off his own laziness or pride; for it is usually through these vices that a leader earns either the contempt or the hatred of his people. Let him live innocently on his own means, adjust his spending to his income, and restrain crimes. He should prevent problems through the proper education of his people rather than allowing evils to increase only to punish them later. 

He should not rashly revive laws that have been abolished by custom, especially those that have long been forgotten and never missed. Nor should he ever seize anything under the guise of a fine, if a judge would not allow a private citizen to take such a thing on the grounds that it was unjust and deceitful.

<margin>A wonderful law of the Macarensians</margin> At this point, I might propose to them the law of the <term>Macarensians</term> <gloss>a fictional people whose name is derived from the Greek word for 'blessed'</gloss>, who also live not very far from Utopia. Their king, on the very first day he enters his reign, is bound by an oath, after great sacrifices have been offered, that he will never have more than a thousand pounds of gold in his treasury at any one time, or an amount of silver equal in value to that gold. <summary>Raphael Hythloday argues that a king's dignity comes from ruling a prosperous people rather than beggars, and describes the Macarensians' law that limits the royal treasury to prevent tyranny.</summary>
<keywords>Fabricius, Macarensians, royal treasury, poverty, kingship, social reform, greed, Utopia</keywords>
